inline.s: From here, the third, makes clear what it draws in. It draws in the sentient beings of the ten directions who have karmic affinity, to be reborn together in that land, transforming and benefiting them through the Dharma. Yet what is drawn in below answers the forty-eight great vows made above, each one separately corresponding, and their mutual relationship can be understood. The text has four divisions: first, it draws in those below to be born together in that land; second, from “the majestic virtue of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life is without limit” onward, it draws in those above to go and be reborn in that land; third, from “the bodhisattvas of that land shall all be destined for the stage of one more birth” onward, it again draws in those below to be born together in that land; fourth, from “Maitreya asked the Buddha how many bodhisattvas of this world would be born there” onward, it again draws in those above to be born together in that land. What is the difference between the first and the third? In the earlier first division the birth-karma is fully explained and rebirth is taught; in the third division gain and loss are set forth to encourage people to be reborn there. Since the meaning differs in this way, they must be distinguished. What is the difference between the second and the fourth? In the earlier second, those above are drawn in to go there together; in the fourth, they are drawn in to be born there together. Since there is this difference, they must be spoken of separately. That it draws in those below makes clear the benefit conferred; that it draws in those above reveals that land's superiority and increases people's yearning for it.

The first has three parts. First, it shows that those born there dwell in the right concentration, leading people to long for it. Second, from “the Buddhas of the ten directions all praise together” onward, it cites those who hear the Name, that they all attain rebirth, increasing people's resolve to go. Third, from “The Buddha told Ananda” onward, it properly distinguishes the birth-karma and teaches the practice of rebirth.

The Buddha told Ananda: “The sentient beings born in that land all dwell in the gathering of right concentration. Why is that? In that Buddha-land there are no gatherings of the erroneous or of the indeterminate.”

[Commentary] In the first division, that those born in that land all dwell in right concentration makes clear what is drawn in. People have three gatherings: first, erroneous concentration; second, right concentration; third, indeterminate. In the Lesser Vehicle the treatises differ. According to the Abhidharma, the ordinary person who is always sinking is called erroneous concentration; the five-stopping contemplation, the general and particular mindfulness, and the two minds of soft and top are called indeterminate, and because these can regress they are called indeterminate; from the mind of endurance onward, firm and unregressing, is called right concentration. According to the Satyasiddhi, the ordinary person who is always sinking is called erroneous concentration; the two wisdoms of hearing and reflection, whose practice can regress, are spoken of as capable of regression; the five-stopping contemplation is called the wisdom of hearing, the general and particular mindfulness the wisdom of reflection, and from soft and top onward is called the wisdom of cultivation; seeing directly that dharmas are empty and never regressing, all of it is right concentration. In the Great Vehicle, before the stage of good destiny is called erroneous concentration; within the stage of good destiny, advancing and retreating many times, is called indeterminate; from the stage of the seed of practice onward, the stage does not regress, and is called right concentration. Whether the sentient beings of the Great Vehicle or of the Lesser Vehicle, those born in that land all dwell in right concentration. Below it explains why: there is no erroneous concentration nor the indeterminate gathering, so all are right.

The Tathagatas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all together praise the majestic spiritual power and merit of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life as inconceivable. All sentient beings who hear his Name, with faith and joy, even in a single thought, with a sincere heart turn their merit and vow to be born in that land, immediately attain rebirth, and dwell in non-retrogression — except only those who commit the five heinous wrongs and slander the true Dharma.

[Commentary] In the second division, first it shows that the Tathagatas of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges all together praise the Buddha of Immeasurable Life; next it shows that sentient beings who hear the Name, have faith, and turn their merit and make vows all attain rebirth; below it reveals the differentiation: excepting only the five heinous wrongs and those who slander the true Dharma, all others are born there. As for the five heinous wrongs: killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing an arhat, breaking the harmony of the sangha, and causing blood to flow from a Buddha's body — these are the five. These five all go against kindness and violate the field of blessing, so they are called heinous. The first two are acts against kindness; the latter three violate the field of blessing. To uphold the false and destroy the right is called slandering the Dharma. Because these obstructions are heavy, they are excluded. Someone asks: In the Contemplation Sutra it is said that even those who commit such wrongs can attain rebirth, yet this sutra says they cannot be born there. How is this explained? There are two meanings. First, distinguishing by person: people are of two kinds. One kind, who long ago aroused the Great Vehicle mind, encounter circumstances and commit the wrongs, like King Ajatashatru and others; though they commit the wrongs, they must have deep repentance, and, arousing the mind, seek to escape, which can extinguish the heavy offenses — hence they attain rebirth, and the Contemplation Sutra is based on this. The other kind, who previously did not arouse the great mind and now commit the heinous offenses, mostly lack deep repentance and cannot resolutely arouse bodhicitta — hence they are not born there, and this sutra is based on this. Second, distinguishing by practice: practice has concentration and scattering. Though some commit the heinous wrongs, they can cultivate the sixteen contemplations of true goodness and deeply contemplate the Buddha's virtue, which extinguishes the heavy offenses, and so attain rebirth — the Contemplation Sutra is based on this. If a person commits the wrongs and cannot cultivate the Buddha-contemplation samadhi, though he does other good it cannot extinguish the offenses, so he is not reborn there — this sutra is based on this.
The Buddha told Ananda: “The gods and humans of the ten directions who, with sincere heart, wish to be born in that land are of three grades.”

[Commentary] The third properly distinguishes the birth-karma and teaches the practice of rebirth. Within it, first it says that the gods and humans of the ten directions who wish to be born in that land are of three grades, giving a general statement. As in the Contemplation Sutra, roughly divided into three, finely into nine. Roughly divided into three, they are the upper, middle, and lower. Among persons of the Great Vehicle, from the stage of the seed of practice onward is called the upper grade; among persons of the Lesser Vehicle, the ordinary person who keeps the precepts, up to the once-returner, are the middle grade; among persons of the Great Vehicle, the ordinary person of the stage of good destiny is called the lower grade. Finely divided into nine, within the upper grade it is further divided into three: the upper-upper, upper-middle, and upper-lower. From the fourth ground onward is called upper-upper, for born there one immediately attains the patient acceptance of non-arising; the first, second, and third grounds are called upper-middle, for born there, after one small eon one attains the patient acceptance of non-arising — the days of that land are long, so within one small eon one attains it, whereas in this world it takes immeasurable eons. The lineage and the stage of understanding and practice are called upper-lower; born there, after three small eons one attains the hundred Dharma-doors and dwells on the first ground. Thus we know that before the ground, too, because the days of that land are long, it takes three small eons to reach the first ground, whereas in this world it takes immeasurable eons.

(Here the stages are judged too high, and do not accord with the intent of drawing in those below. Examining the text on the upper grade in the Contemplation Sutra, it is also ordinary beings of great mind who, relying on their vows, are reborn. One should accord with the Perfect Teaching, and at the fullness of the ten stages of faith, be born in the upper-upper grade, and at that time enter the first stage of abiding — as the Avatamsaka Sutra says, proving all is proven, that is, at the first arousing of the mind one attains right enlightenment. This alone accords with the subtle meaning of this sutra. The commentator, following the Gradual Teaching, judged it as the stages of the grounds for the upper grade, fearing this might cause later people to doubt and think ordinary beings have no share; therefore I briefly discuss it.)

The middle-grade persons are also divided into three: the middle-upper, middle-middle, and middle-lower. From the seeing of the path onward is called middle-upper, for born there one immediately attains the arhat fruit. The inner ordinary person is called middle-middle, for born there one immediately attains the stream-enterer fruit. The four minds from “warm” onward are called the inner ordinary; the outer ordinary person who keeps the precepts is called middle-lower, for born there, after one small eon one attains the arhat. The lower-grade persons are also divided into three: the lower-upper, lower-middle, and lower-lower. There they are divided by the lightness or heaviness of the offenses done, not by their stages. The nine grades there are here combined into three: the three persons of the upper grade combine into the upper class, the three of the middle grade into the middle class, and the three of the lower grade into the lower class. Though the pursuits of these three classes differ, when it comes to wishing to be born there, all must arouse the mind and seek great bodhi, single-mindedly think of that Buddha, turn their merit and make vows, and only then attain rebirth; hence this is discussed. A question: Vasubandhu, in composing the verses on rebirth, says that women, those with deficient faculties, and those of the two-vehicle seeds all cannot be born there; yet the Contemplation Sutra declares that beings of the Lesser Vehicle also attain rebirth. How is this explained? The explanation: that statement that women and those with deficient faculties cannot be born there is spoken from the standpoint of receiving the retribution within that land, for there are no women there nor those with deficient faculties. The statement that those of the two-vehicle seed cannot be born there is spoken from the standpoint of going from this land; Lesser Vehicle beings, though they previously studied the Lesser Vehicle, when about to depart must arouse the great mind to attain rebirth; if with the small mind they seek birth in that land, there is no principle of going. Hence Vasubandhu says the two-vehicle seed cannot attain rebirth. A question: if the departure uses the great mind, why upon arrival do they realize the small fruit? The explanation: because of their long habituation to the Lesser Vehicle; originally here they studied much the contemplation of suffering and impermanence, and upon arrival, hearing of suffering and impermanence, they immediately awaken and understand, and so realize the small fruit. Because in the end they aroused the great mind to seek birth there, having attained the arhat there they immediately seek the great. Above was the general statement; below it is shown separately.

As for the upper class: they abandon the home and put aside desire, becoming monastics; they arouse bodhicitta; they single-mindedly think of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life; they cultivate various merits; and they vow to be born in that land. When these beings approach the end of life, the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, together with the great assembly, appears before them; they then follow that Buddha and are born in his land, and in the seven-jeweled lotus they are spontaneously transformed and born; they dwell in non-retrogression, with wisdom brave and fierce, and spiritual powers effortless. Therefore, Ananda, whatever beings wish to see the Buddha of Immeasurable Life in this present life should arouse the mind of supreme bodhi, cultivate merit and virtue, and vow to be born in that land.

[Commentary] Within the upper class, first it states, then distinguishes, then concludes with praise. In the distinguishing there are three: first it sets forth their cultivation of the causal practice; second, from “these beings” onward, they together accomplish rebirth; third, from “dwelling in non-retrogression” onward, the benefit they gain in that land. In the initial cause of cultivation there are five clauses: first, leaving the world and the home; second, arousing bodhicitta; third, single-mindedly thinking of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life; fourth, cultivating various merits; fifth, using the aforementioned goodness to vow birth in that land. In the rebirth, first that Buddha welcomes them, then from “they follow” onward, this going to and being born in that land; in the benefit, dwelling in non-retrogression — the stage is firm; wisdom brave, and so on — the accomplished virtue is supreme. Above was the statement, next the distinguishing, and from “therefore” onward the concluding praise of the practice.

The Buddha told Ananda: “As for the middle class: the gods and humans of the ten directions who, with sincere heart, wish to be born in that land — though they cannot act as monastics or greatly cultivate merit, they should arouse the mind of supreme bodhi, single-mindedly think of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, and in some measure cultivate goodness: receive and observe the precepts and the pure fasts, erect stupas and images, feed monastics, hang pennants and light lamps, scatter flowers and burn incense; and turning this merit, vow to be born in that land. When such a person approaches the end of life, the Buddha of Immeasurable Life manifests his body, in light and marks and appearance fully like the true Buddha, and together with the great assembly appears before him; he then follows the transformed Buddha and is born in that land, dwelling in non-retrogression, with merit and wisdom next to those of the upper class.”

[Commentary] Within the middle class, first it states, then distinguishes. In distinguishing, again first it sets forth their causal practice, next the rebirth, then reveals the benefit. In the first statement of the cause: the gods and humans of the ten directions who with sincere heart wish birth in that land — a general statement. “Though they cannot act as monastics, etc.” distinguishes them from the upper class. According to the Contemplation Sutra, these are Lesser Vehicle persons, and so they cannot greatly cultivate merit there. From “they should arouse” onward it properly distinguishes their cause, with four clauses: first, arouse bodhicitta; second, single-mindedly think of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life; third, cultivate a little merit and goodness; fourth, turn the merit and vow birth. Though such a person previously studied the Lesser Vehicle, when truly wishing to be born there he must cultivate these four practices, and only then attains rebirth. In the rebirth, first that Buddha welcomes him, then he is born there; the benefit can be understood.

The Buddha told Ananda: “As for the lower class: the gods and humans of the ten directions who, with sincere heart, wish to be born in that land — even if they cannot do various merits, they should arouse the mind of supreme bodhi, single-mindedly direct their attention, and even to ten thoughts, think on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, and vow to be born in his land. If they hear the profound Dharma and rejoice with faith and joy, giving rise to no doubt, and even in a single thought think on that Buddha, and with a most sincere heart vow to be born in that land, then at the end of life, dreaming of that Buddha, they too attain rebirth, with merit and wisdom next to those of the middle class.”

[Commentary] Within the lower class, first it states, then distinguishes. In distinguishing, again first it sets forth their causal practice, next the rebirth, then reveals the benefit. In the first statement of the cause: the gods and humans of the ten directions who with sincere heart wish birth in that land — a general statement. “Even if they cannot do various merits” distinguishes them from the middle class. As in the Contemplation Sutra, the offenses are cited to distinguish; here it is briefly omitted. From “they should arouse” onward it properly distinguishes their cause, with four names: first, arouse bodhicitta; second, single-mindedly think of that Buddha of Immeasurable Life, even to ten thoughts, and vow birth in that land; third, hearing the profound Dharma, rejoice with faith and joy, giving rise to no doubt; fourth, with a most sincere heart, even in a single thought think on that Buddha, and vow birth in that land — they too attain rebirth. In the rebirth, it shows that dreaming of that Buddha at the end of life, one also attains rebirth; the benefit can be understood.
Above, the first division set forth drawing in those below.

From here, the second division sets forth drawing in those above to be reborn together in that land. It is cited to reveal the superiority of Amitabha's land and to increase the resolve of the lower people to seek rebirth. Within it, first the prose briefly explains, then the verses expand the discussion.

The Buddha told Ananda: “The majestic spiritual power of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life is without limit. The Tathagatas of the ten directions, immeasurable and boundless and inconceivable, all without exception praise him. In the east, in Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the immeasurable and countless assemblies of bodhisattvas all go to the place of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, and respectfully make offerings, together with the assemblies of bodhisattvas and shravakas, hearing and receiving the sutras and Dharma, and proclaiming the teaching of the Way. So likewise in the south, west, and north, in the four directions and above and below.”

[Commentary] In the earlier prose there are two divisions: first, the Buddhas all praise together; second, from “in the east” onward, the bodhisattvas together go and are born. The later verses separately praise them; one should carefully note this. In the earlier Buddha-praise: first the Buddha told Ananda that the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life is without limit — Sakyamuni praising himself; from “the ten directions” onward, the other Buddhas praise together. Below, these are separately sung; one should also note it. In the going-together below, first the east is listed, then the other directions are analogized. In listing the east: in the eastern Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges the countless bodhisattvas all go to the Buddha of Immeasurable Life — this is the beginning. Respectfully making offerings, together with the assemblies of bodhisattvas and shravakas — this is the next. Hearing and receiving the sutras and Dharma, and proclaiming the teaching of the Way — this is the end. Since the east is thus, the other directions are also so. This beginning, middle, and end are separately sung in the verses below; one should also note it. The verses below sing it.
At that time the World-Honored One spoke verses, saying:

The World-Honored One spoke verses — the sutra's compiler sets this out. Below is the actual singing. There are thirty verses. The first fifteen sing of the earlier latter division, the bodhisattvas going together; the last fifteen sing of the earlier first division, the Buddhas praising together.

Of the first fifteen, the first two verses sing of the going together above; then five verses sing of the respectful making of offerings in the earlier text; below, eight verses sing of the earlier hearing of the Dharma and proclaiming of the teaching.
In eastern Buddha-lands,
as many as Ganges' sands, the bodhisattvas of those realms all go to see the Immeasurable One.
South, west, and north, the four,
above and below likewise: the bodhisattva hosts of those lands all go to see the Immeasurable One.

[Commentary] Of the first two verses, the first sings of the earlier going-together in the east, and the latter sings of the going-together in the remaining directions. Arriving there, they respectfully greet the Buddha of Immeasurable Life; hence it is called “beholding the Immeasurable Enlightened One.”
All the bodhisattvas,
each bearing heavenly wondrous flowers, precious incense and priceless garments, make offerings to the Immeasurable One.
Together they sound celestial music,
pouring forth gentle and harmonious tones, singing praise of the most supreme One, making offering to the Immeasurable One.
Having reached the depths of spiritual powers and wisdom,
they roam into the deep gates of Dharma, complete in the treasury of merit, with wondrous wisdom without peer.
The sun of wisdom illumines the world,
dispelling the clouds of birth and death; in reverence they circle three times and bow before the supreme One.
They see that land, adorned and pure,
subtle and wonderful beyond thought, and so arouse the measureless resolve: “may my land be likewise.”

[Commentary] Of the next five verses, the first four speak of seeing the Buddha and making offerings, and the last one of seeing the land and forming the wish. Of the first four, the first two speak of outer offerings to things, and the latter two of inner offerings. In the outer offerings: each bearing wondrous flowers is an offering; the precious is an offering of treasure; the incense is an offering of incense; the priceless garments are an offering by clothing; the sounding of celestial music and so forth is an offering of music; and within the tones of music they sing praise of the Buddha's virtue. In the inner offerings, the first verse and a half speak of the offering of praise by speech, and the latter half verse of reverent offering by the body. In the praise by speech, the first verse praises the Buddha's own virtue, and the latter half verse praises the Buddha's benefiting of others. In praising his own virtue: reaching the depths of spiritual powers and wisdom and roaming into the deep Dharma praises the Buddha's two virtues of wisdom and spiritual powers. Wisdom is the root of spiritual powers, and spiritual powers are the function of wisdom; the two are mutually dependent, so both are praised. The perfection of the spiritual powers and wisdom is called “reaching the depths”; being wholly complete is called “utter,” and being thorough is called “attaining.” These spiritual powers and wisdom both arise in accordance with the Dharma, so again it shows the roaming into the deep Dharma: to dwell in contemplation is called “roaming,” and to exhaust the source is called “entering”; realizing the realm of Dharma of the dependent-rising gate, one can manifest supreme spiritual powers, and realizing the realm of Dharma of the wisdom gate, one can raise up supreme wisdom. Complete in the treasury of merit with wondrous wisdom without peer praises the Buddha's two practices of fortune and wisdom. Fortune is the support of wisdom, and wisdom is the guide of fortune; the two are mutually dependent, so both are praised. The practice of fortune fully complete is called “endowed with the treasury of merit,” and the wisdom-practice supreme is called “wisdom without peer.” “Peer” means a match; there is no match for the Buddha, so it is called “without peer.” In the latter benefiting of others: the sun of wisdom illumining the world transforms people and gives rise to wisdom; wisdom can awaken and illumine like the sun, teaching people to gain understanding, so it is called “ilumining the world.” Dispelling birth and death transforms people and removes obstructions; birth and death cover and obstruct, and from a metaphor it is spoken of as “clouds.” The reverent bowing by the body is understood. The four verses above speak of seeing the Buddha and making offerings; the verse below speaks of seeing the land and forming the wish; the text is clear and can be understood.
Then the Immeasurable One,
his countenance moved, issued a joyful smile; from his mouth countless lights streamed, illumining the lands of the ten directions.
Turning back the light to encircle his body,
three times it circled and entered the crown; all the hosts of gods and humans, leaping, rejoiced with joy.
The great being, Guanyin,
arranging his robes and bowing, asked: “Tell me, O Buddha, what cause of this smile? We beg you, we wish you to explain the meaning.”
His Brahma-sound like thunder's roll,
the eight tones pouring out wondrous sound: “I shall bestow the bodhisattva's prophecy; now hear it, O virtuous ones, and listen well.”
The true sages come from the ten directions;
I know all their vows: seeking to adorn a pure land, they receive the prophecy and shall become Buddhas.
Awake to all dharmas,
as dream, illusion, and echo, fulfilling all the wondrous vows, they shall surely attain such a land.
Knowing dharmas as lightning and shadows,
they carry the bodhisattva-way to its end; with their root of merit and virtue, they receive the prophecy and shall become Buddhas.
Penetrating the nature of all dharmas,
all empty and without self, seeking the pure Buddha-land with compassion, they shall surely attain such a land.

[Commentary] These eight verses sing of the earlier hearing of the Dharma and proclaiming of the teaching. In this text, the first two verses show the Tathagata Amitabha manifesting a sign to initiate; then one verse has Guanyin ask in wonder; and the last five verses have that Buddha answer fully. “The Brahma-sound like thunder” and “the eight tones pouring out wondrous sound” answer in praise of the wondrousness of the sound. The eight Brahma-tones, as the Brahma-deva-parable Sutra explains: first the most wondrous sound, whose tone is sorrowful and beautiful; second the easily-understood sound, whose words are clearly distinguished; third the harmonious sound, whose loud and soft are measured; fourth the gentle sound, whose tone is gentle; fifth the unerring sound, whose words have no error; sixth the unwomanish sound, whose tone is virile and resounding; seventh the honored-and-wise sound, whose words have dignity and awe, like the sound of a respected and wise person in the world; eighth the deep and far sound, whose tone is deep and far like the rolling of thunder. With this wondrous sound he answers Guanyin: “I shall bestow the bodhisattva's prophecy; now hear it, O virtuous ones, and listen well” — commanding them to listen and permitting the explanation. The words of the prophecy are as explained above. “Now I shall speak this; do you, virtuous ones, listen well.” From here, four verses set forth what is actually said. In them, the first verse raises their vow-mind and prophesies certain Buddhahood. The second verse raises their wisdom and vow and prophesies certain attainment of the land: “awake to all as dream and illusion, etc.” raises their wisdom; “fulfilling all the wondrous vows” raises their vow; “shall attain such a land” prophesies the attainment. The third verse raises their wisdom and practice, prophesying certain Buddhahood: “knowing dharmas as lightning” raises their wisdom; “carrying the bodhisattva-way to its end and having all the roots of virtue” raises their practice; “receiving the prophecy and becoming Buddha” prophesies the attainment. The fourth verse raises their wisdom and vow, prophesying certain attainment of the land: “penetrating the nature of all dharmas and all empty and without self” raises their wisdom — the earlier “awake to all as dream and illusion, etc.” is the wisdom of worldly truth, while this “penetrating the nature of all dharmas and all empty without self” is the wisdom of ultimate truth; “seeking the pure land with compassion” raises their vow; “shall attain such a land” prophesies the attainment.

The last fifteen verses sing of the Buddhas' praising together in the earlier text. The first five sing of the earlier Buddhas of the ten directions all praising together; the last ten sing of the earlier Sakyamuni praising himself.
The Buddhas announce to the bodhisattvas:
“Now go and behold the Buddha of Peaceful Nurture; hearing the Dharma, rejoice and receive and practice, and quickly attain the pure abode.”
Arriving at that land, adorned and pure,
they quickly attain spiritual powers, and surely from the Immeasurable One receive the prophecy and become enlightened ones.
The power of that Buddha's original vows:
hearing the Name and wishing to be reborn, all reach that land, and are settled in non-retrogression.
The bodhisattvas rouse surpassing vows:
may their own land be no different; with universal thought they save all, and their names fill the ten directions.
Serving countless Tathagatas,
flying and transforming through all lands, respectfully and joyfully departing, they return to the land of Peaceful Nurture.

[Commentary] Of the first five verses, the Buddhas announce to the bodhisattvas, commanding them to behold the land of Peaceful Nurture — this is the direct exhortation to go. “Hearing the Dharma and receiving and practicing” shows what is done upon going. “Quickly attaining” and below shows the benefit of doing so: “quickly attaining the pure abode” shows the benefit of the earlier hearing of the Dharma, receiving, and practicing; in the future getting a wondrous pure land is called “attaining the pure abode.” The four verses below reveal the benefit of the earlier going to behold the land of Peaceful Nurture; the benefit has five kinds. First, the benefit of attaining spiritual powers there — the first half verse. Second, the benefit of receiving the prophecy there — the next half verse; previously it was said that that Buddha prophesies to the bodhisattvas, which is just this matter. Third, the benefit of attaining non-retrogression there — the next verse; previously it was said that being born there one dwells in the right concentration, which is just this matter. Fourth, the benefit of rousing vows there — the next verse; “the bodhisattvas rouse surpassing vows” is the general statement, and below it is separately praised. In the separate praise, “may their own land be no different” is the vow of seeking a pure land, the vow to attain a land like Amitabha's, called “no different”; “with universal thought saving all” is the vow of transforming sentient beings; “their names fill the ten directions” is the vow of seeking the Buddha-body, the vow that when they become Buddhas their names reach the ten directions. Fifth, the benefit of broadly serving many Buddhas and rousing practice there — the last verse.

From here, ten verses have Sakyamuni praising himself, to lead people to go together. Within it there are three parts: the first three verses raise the difficulty of hearing the sutra and the joy of practicing; the next four verses praise the Buddha Amitabha's giving of prophecy to the bodhisattvas, that is, the supreme excellence of his Buddha-wisdom, leading people to turn and take refuge; and the last three verses exhort by principle.
If a person has no mind of goodness,
he cannot hear this sutra; those pure in precepts may gain the hearing of true Dharma.
One who has seen the World-Honored One before,
can then trust in this matter; with humility and respect he hears, receives, and practices, leaping with great joy.
The arrogant and the evil, the indolent,
can hardly trust this Dharma; those who in former lives saw the Buddhas delight to hear such teaching.

[Commentary] Of the first three verses, the first half verse raises the person without goodness who does not hear this sutra, revealing the profundity and weight of the sutra; then a verse and a half raises the person with goodness who at last gains the hearing, showing the subtlety of the sutra. Within it, first it shows that the person with goodness gains the hearing of this sutra; from “one who has seen” onward it shows that the one who has seen the Buddha can then believe, revere, rejoice, and practice. The next half verse raises the person with evil who does not believe this Dharma, revealing its depth and weight. The half verse below raises the one with goodness who delights to hear this teaching, showing its subtlety. Raising the evil who do not hear leads people to reject and distance themselves; raising the good who gain the hearing leads people to long to practice. Moreover, this text reveals the depth and weight of the sutra to dispel people's light disrespect, and shows its subtlety to give rise to people's faith and reverence.
Whether shravaka or bodhisattva,
none can fathom the sage's mind; it is like one born blind who would go and be a guide to others.
The Buddha's sea of wisdom,
deep and vast without bottom or shore; the two vehicles cannot measure it; only the Buddha alone knows it clearly.
Suppose all people,
fully attained the Way, their pure wisdom like the original emptiness, pondering the Buddha's wisdom for a billion eons,
exhausting their strength in utmost discourse,
even to the end of life they would not know it; the Buddha's wisdom is without bound, and thus brings them to purity.

[Commentary] These four verses praise the supreme excellence of the Buddha Amitabha's wisdom and virtue, leading people to turn and take refuge. Within them, the first seven sentences show that the shravakas and bodhisattvas cannot measure it: first the principle, next the simile, then the combining, as can be understood. Then one sentence shows that the Buddha alone knows it. Then six sentences show that all people, having attained the holy Way, together think upon it and know it not: “suppose all people” shows the many; “fully attaining the Way” shows the excellence of their conduct and virtue; “pure wisdom reaching the root” shows the depth of the empty understanding; “pondering the Buddha's wisdom for a billion eons” shows the long contemplation; “exhausting strength in utmost discourse” shows the uttermost of words; yet even so, “to the end of life they would not know it.” The half verse below concludes and praises its superiority: “the Buddha's wisdom without bound” praises the breadth of the Buddha's wisdom; “thus bringing them to purity” praises the purity of the Buddha's virtue. “Bringing” means arriving; reaching to the purity of the Dharma-nature and nirvana, so it is hard to measure and know.
Life is very hard to gain; a Buddha's world also is hard to encounter. The mind of faith and wisdom is hard; if one hears this, one should strive with diligence.
Hearing the Dharma, one does not forget; seeing and revering, one gains the great rejoicing. Then one is my good friend and benefactor; therefore one should rouse the resolve.
Though the whole world were filled with fire, one must pass through it to hear the Dharma; one shall surely accomplish the Buddha-way and broadly save the stream of birth and death.

[Commentary] These three verses exhort by principle. Of them, the first verse raises the three difficulties and urges people to seek diligently: life being hard to gain is the first difficulty; a Buddha's world being hard to encounter is the second; having the mind of faith and wisdom being hard is the third. These three difficulties one has now gained, so having heard this sutra one should diligently seek. The next verse raises the benefit from seeing and hearing, urging people to arouse the mind: hearing without forgetting means hearing the Dharma without forgetting at the place of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life; seeing and revering means seeing the Buddha of Immeasurable Life and giving rise to profound reverence; gaining the great rejoicing means the good benefit of the earlier hearing the Dharma, seeing the Buddha, and revering him; gaining the good and being joyful is called gaining the great rejoicing. “Then one is my good friend” means being taken in by the Buddha; practicing in accord with Sakyamuni is called being my good friend; “therefore one should rouse” is the concluding exhortation to arouse the resolve. The last verse teaches the resolute going: “though the whole world were filled with fire, one must pass through it to hear the Dharma” shows the resolute decision to go; “one shall surely accomplish Buddhahood and broadly save the stream of birth and death” shows what one goes for: to surely accomplish Buddhahood is to seek the fruit of self-benefit, and to broadly save the stream of birth and death is to seek the fruit of benefiting others.
The Commentary on the Meaning of the Sutra of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, Scroll Four, End

blocks.text: The Commentary on the Meaning of the Sutra of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, Scroll Five

inline.s: From here, the third, again draws in those below to be born together in that land. Within it there are three: first, it broadly raises the supremely wonderful affairs of the land of Immeasurable Life to make people wish for it; second, from “the worldly people of shallow customs” onward, it reveals the Saha world to be full of defilement and evil, making people weary and abandon it; third, from “broadly reverencing the Immeasurable” onward, taking the land of Amitabha it distinguishes gain and loss, leading people to cultivate and to abandon.

Within the first there are two: first, it broadly raises the affairs of supreme joy in the land of Immeasurable Life; second, from “the Buddha told Maitreya and the gods and humans” onward, it urges people to be reborn there. In the former there are eight: first, it shows that the life in that land is long; second, it shows the supreme marvelousness of their light; third, it shows that their bodies and marks are complete; fourth, it shows the supreme excellence of their wisdom and virtue; fifth, it shows that those born there forever leave the evil destinies; sixth, it shows that they offer many things in that land; seventh, it shows that their hearing of the Dharma is uninterrupted; eighth, it shows that the practice and virtue of the bodhisattvas there are fully complete.

The Buddha told Ananda: “The bodhisattvas of that land shall all be destined for the stage of one more birth, excepting those whose original vows, for the sake of sentient beings, adorn themselves with the merit of the great vow and universally desire to deliver all sentient beings.”

[Commentary] In the first division, it shows that those bodhisattvas shall all be destined for the stage of one more birth, revealing the long life with no untimely death, excepting those who, for the sake of beings, receive bodies in other lands.

“Ananda, in that Buddha-land the assemblies of shravakas have a body-light of a fathom, and the bodhisattvas' light illumines a hundred yojanas. There are two bodhisattvas, most honored and supreme, whose majestic spiritual light universally illumines the three-thousand great-thousand world. Ananda said to the Buddha: ‘What are the names of those two bodhisattvas?’ The Buddha said: ‘One is called Guanyin, the other Mahasthamaprapta. These two bodhisattvas, in this land, cultivated the bodhisattva-way, and at the end of life, transformed, were born in that Buddha-land.’”

[Commentary] In the second division, first it shows that the shravakas of that land have a body-light of a fathom; next it shows that the other bodhisattvas there illumine a hundred yojanas — one yojana is forty li, so a hundred yojanas is four thousand li; and third, it reveals that Guanyin and Mahasthamaprapta illumine the three-thousand great-thousand world. Within it, first it distinguishes, then from “Ananda said to the Buddha” it distinguishes their names; and from “these two bodhisattvas, in this land” onward it shows that they were born from this land.
“Ananda, the sentient beings born in that land all possess the thirty-two marks in full.”
[Commentary] In the third division, it shows that the bodies and marks of those born there are complete, all possessing the thirty-two marks, as extensively set forth in the sutra.

“Their wisdom is complete and fulfilled; they penetrate deeply into all dharmas, exhaust and express the essential mysterious meaning; their spiritual powers are without obstruction; their faculties are all bright and sharp. Those of dull faculties attain the two kinds of patient acceptance; those of sharp faculties attain the incalculable patient acceptance of non-arising.”

[Commentary] In the fourth division, it shows the supreme excellence of the wisdom and virtue of those born there. The sentences are four: first, wisdom complete and fulfilled, penetrating deeply into all dharmas, realizing the Dharma-nature, exhausting and expressing the essential mysterious meaning, reaching the marrow of the teaching; second, spiritual powers without obstruction; third, all faculties bright and sharp; fourth, the patient acceptance differs: those of dull faculties accomplish two kinds of patient acceptance, namely the patient acceptance of sound and the patient acceptance of compliance; those of sharp faculties, up to and including the attainment of Buddhahood, attain the asamkhya patient acceptance of non-arising.

“Moreover, those bodhisattvas, up to the attainment of Buddhahood, do not receive the evil destinies; they have spiritual powers at ease and always know their former lives, excepting when, to transform beings, they are born in other pure lands of the five turbidities of the evil world, manifesting in harmony with those lands, as in my land.”

[Commentary] In the fifth division, it shows that those born there forever leave the evil destinies. Within it, first it shows that those born in that land, up to and including the attainment of Buddhahood, no longer fall into the evil destinies, having spiritual powers at ease and always knowing their former lives; later, excepting when, for the sake of beings, they are born in other lands, Sakyamuni says this himself, as with the bodhisattvas of his own land.

The Buddha spoke to Ananda: “Those bodhisattvas of that land, relying on the Buddha's majestic spiritual power, in the space of one meal, go to the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions and respectfully make offerings to the Buddha World-Honored Ones. According to what the mind thinks, flowers and incense, music, canopies, umbrellas, banners, and countless immeasurable offerings are spontaneously transformed and produced, responding to the thought and arriving. Wondrous and precious, supremely special, not what the world has, they scatter them over all the Buddhas and the assemblies of bodhisattvas and shravakas. In the sky they transform into flower-canopies, their light and color shining brilliantly, their fragrance pervading all. The flowers, four hundred li around and so on, doubling and trebling, spread over the three-thousand great-thousand world. Following their order, they transform and vanish in turn. Those bodhisattvas, all together joyful, in the sky jointly play celestial music, and with subtle and wondrous sounds sing praise of the Buddha's virtue. Hearing and receiving the sutras and Dharma, their joy is measureless. Having made offering to the Buddha, before eating, suddenly lightly lifting, they return to their own land.”

[Commentary] In the sixth division, it shows that those born there can offer extensive offerings. Within it, first it shows their going to the ten directions to offer extensively to many Buddhas; next, from the receiving of the Dharma, and later it shows that while the meal is not yet eaten they return to their own land. In the former there are four clauses: first, it shows that those bodhisattvas of that land, within the space of one meal, go to the ten directions and offer to all the Buddhas; second, from “according to the mind” onward, it shows the offerings transforming in accord with the mind; third, from “in the sky” onward, it shows them transforming into flower-canopies in the sky; fourth, from “those bodhisattvas” onward, it shows the bodhisattvas jointly playing celestial music and singing praise of the Buddha's virtue. “All” means all; all rejoicing and leaping is called “all joyful.” And having made offering to the Buddha, before the meal is eaten, they return to their own land.

The Buddha spoke to Ananda: “When the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, for the shravakas, bodhisattvas, gods, and humans, proclaims the Dharma, they all assemble in the seven-jeweled hall; widely proclaiming the teaching of the Way, and expounding the wonderful Dharma, none but rejoice, the mind attaining understanding and the Way. At that time, from the four directions a wind naturally arises, blowing the seven-jeweled trees, which give forth the five kinds of sound; measureless wonderful flowers, drifting with the wind and scattering in the four directions, naturally make offering, without ceasing. All the gods bring hundreds and thousands of celestial flowers and incense, and ten thousand kinds of music, to offer to that Buddha and the assemblies of bodhisattvas and shravakas. Universally scattering flowers and incense, they play all the music; coming and going, each giving way to the other. At that time, peacefully joyful, the happiness cannot be told.”

[Commentary] In the seventh division, it shows that the hearing of the Dharma by those born there is uninterrupted. Within it, first when the Dharma is spoken, the assembly gathers in the hall and the Tathagata preaches; from “none but” onward it shows the benefit of the preaching: the mind attaining understanding and the Way. From “at that time” onward it sets up the offering to the Buddha; within it, first the wind shakes the trees to give sound, next it blows the wonderful flowers, and later the gods and so forth hold flowers and incense and music, offering and presenting, with entertainment without end.

From here, the eighth shows that the practice and virtue of those bodhisattvas are fully complete. Within it, first the particulars, later the general conclusion. In the particulars there are seven: first, the practice cultivating away from transgression; second, from “fully endowed” onward, the accomplished virtue fully complete; third, from “equal contemplation of the three worlds as empty and non-existent” onward, the practice is fully accomplished; fourth, from “thoroughly the One Vehicle” onward, the accomplished virtue is supremely excellent; fifth, from “destroying jealousy” onward, the practice advances; sixth, from “the power of causes” onward, all powers are complete; seventh, from “the marks and good qualities of the body” onward, taking all the virtues together it generally praises and reveals their superiority.

The Buddha told Ananda: “The bodhisattvas born in that Buddha-land, whatever they expound, always proclaim the true Dharma, following wisdom, without transgression and without loss. Toward all things of that land, they have no mind of self-possession, no mind of attachment; going, coming, advancing, stopping, their feelings have no clinging; at ease and free, no preference and no aversion, no self and no other, no contention and no litigation. Toward all sentient beings they gain the mind of great compassion and benefit, gentle and subdued, without a mind of anger and hatred; free of the coverings, pure and clean, without a mind of weariness and neglect; with the equal mind, the superior mind, the deep mind, the concentrated mind, and the mind that loves the Dharma, delights in the Dharma, and rejoices in the Dharma. They extinguish all afflictions, and have the mind that leaves the evil destinies; thorough in all that the bodhisattva practices.”
